definition: In information theory, linguistics, and computer science, the Levenshtein distance is a string metric for measuring the difference between two sequences.
details: For two strings, it is the minimum number of single-symbol edits—insertions, deletions, or substitutions—required to transform one string into the other. Each edit has unit cost in the classical definition. The distance is named after Soviet mathematician Vladimir Levenshtein, who introduced it in 1965 in the context of error-correcting codes. Levenshtein distance is a particular form of edit distance; the latter term is also used for broader models in which the set of allowed operations or their costs differ. It is closely related to sequence alignment.

explainer.lead: Levenshtein distance counts how many single-character changes are needed to turn one string into another. It gives a precise way to compare sequences when insertions, deletions, and substitutions all matter.

tiers.eli5: Imagine changing one word into another using only three moves: add a letter, remove a letter, or swap one letter for another. Levenshtein distance is the smallest number of moves you need. Turning "kitten" into "sitting" takes three moves, so their distance is 3.
tiers.practitioner: Use it when string differences should be expressed as a minimum edit count, with insertion, deletion, and substitution each costing 1. Check whether that unit-cost model fits the task; other edit-distance variants allow different operations or costs. The result measures sequence difference and is closely related to sequence alignment.
tiers.paperLevel: For strings a and b, lev(a,b) is the minimum number of unit-cost insertions, deletions, and substitutions transforming a into b. Its recurrence is lev(i,j) = min(lev(i-1,j)+1, lev(i,j-1)+1, lev(i-1,j-1)+[a_i != b_j]), with lev(i,0)=i and lev(0,j)=j. Vladimir Levenshtein introduced the measure in 1965 in the context of error-correcting codes; its classical form fixes both the allowed operations and their unit costs.

explainer.example: For "kitten" and "sitting", substitute k with s, substitute e with i, then insert g at the end. These three edits give lev("kitten", "sitting") = 3.

explainer.measures: It measures the difference between two strings as the minimum number of single-symbol edits needed to transform one into the other.
howScored: Allow insertion, deletion, and substitution of single symbols.
Assign every edit a cost of 1 in the classical definition.
Find a sequence of edits with the smallest total count.
Report that minimum count as the distance.
explainer.formula: lev(a,b) = minimum number of unit-cost insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform string a into string b.
explainer.typicalResults: The result is a non-negative integer: identical strings have distance 0, while strings requiring more edits have larger distances.
caveats: The classical definition allows only insertions, deletions, and substitutions.
Each operation has unit cost; broader edit-distance models may change operations or costs.
A larger distance means more required edits, not a different kind of sequence relationship.
